content.p: On the morning of Wednesday 16 June 1976, thousands of Black schoolchildren set out from their schools in Soweto, the township outside Johannesburg, to march to Orlando Stadium. They were protesting against a government rule that forced them to be taught partly in Afrikaans. Police met them with tear gas and then live ammunition. By nightfall, buildings and vehicles belonging to the government's West Rand Administration Board were on fire, and the protest had become an uprising that, according to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, lasted fifteen months and reached 200 towns and cities.

How many people died is still argued over. The police said 23 people were killed on 16 June. Other reports put the figure for that day at 200 or more. The government's Cillié Commission later counted 575 deaths over the whole period it examined, and blamed police for 451 of them. A museum exhibit at the University of Michigan gives a range of 176 to 700 dead for the whole uprising. Whatever the exact figure, the dead were mostly young: the Truth Commission found that most of the more than 575 students who died were under twenty-five.
content.h2: A school system built to limit its pupils
content.p: The roots lay in the Bantu Education Act of 1953, which gave central government control of the schooling of Black South Africans and removed it from churches and provincial authorities. Before the Act, about 90 percent of Black schools were state-aided mission schools; almost all of them closed. Hendrik Verwoerd, the Act's architect, said there was "no place for [the African] in the European community above the level of certain forms of labour". The Act also tied spending on African education to the direct taxes Africans paid, so far less was spent on Black children than on white ones.

By the early 1970s the system was under strain. South African History Online records that Soweto got no new high schools from 1962 to 1971, because the government expected pupils to attend schools in their ethnic "homelands". Under pressure from business for a better-trained Black workforce, the government then built 40 new schools in Soweto. Between 1972 and 1976, secondary enrolment there rose from 12,656 to 34,656 pupils, and one in five Soweto children was in secondary school. A large, restless student population now existed, and Black Consciousness ideas were gaining ground among it. The movement took organised form in SASO, the South African Students Organisation, and in the Black People's Convention of 1972.

The government, meanwhile, was closing off protest. According to the Truth Commission's regional profile, in 1973 eight SASO and Black People's Convention leaders were served with five-year banning orders, and in 1974 nine members were convicted under the Terrorism Act although, in the Commission's words, there had been no physical acts of "terrorism".
content.h2: The language decree and the boycotts
content.p: In 1974 the government of Prime Minister B.J. Vorster issued the Afrikaans Medium Decree. As Newsweek describes it, Black schools were to use a 50-50 mixture of English and Afrikaans, with Afrikaans the sole language for subjects including mathematics and social studies. The University of Michigan exhibit adds that the government justified the decree through a clause of the 1909 Union of South Africa Act and the fact that Afrikaans had replaced Dutch as an official language in 1925. The Truth Commission, by contrast, describes a 1975 directive from the Bantu Education Department to schools in the Transvaal that Afrikaans be used on an equal basis with English in secondary schools.

Teachers' associations objected on practical grounds: most pupils did not speak Afrikaans well enough to learn mathematics in it. Pupils and parents also objected on principle. Desmond Tutu, then Bishop of Johannesburg, called Afrikaans the "language of the oppressor". South Africa Gateway notes that English was already pupils' second language, so the decree demanded they learn through a third.

The Truth Commission traced the escalation. The Commission's account starts in February 1976, when two school-board members in Meadowlands lost their posts for defying the order. By May, pupils at Orlando West Junior Secondary School had begun a class boycott after a circuit inspector refused to meet them, and by the end of that month six schools were boycotting. That month, the Commission says, an Afrikaans teacher at Pimville Higher Primary was knifed, and an attempt by police to detain a youth over the attack ended with stones thrown at them. The Commission wrote that the government "appeared reluctant to acknowledge the depth of opposition" despite warnings from several quarters. The Michigan exhibit gives 30 April as the date the Orlando West pupils first stayed away.

At a meeting on 13 June, according to the Michigan exhibit, students from around Soweto formed a Soweto Students' Representative Council, and called a mass rally for 16 June. Dan Montsisi, an Action Committee member, told the Truth Commission that the students saw themselves as fighting a fight their elders had already lost. Murphy Morobe said the committee gave itself only three days to organise and kept the plan from parents and teachers for fear they would try to stop it.
content.h2: The march and the first shots
content.p: Student leaders came mainly from Naledi High, Morris Isaacson High and Phefeni Junior Secondary. South Africa Gateway reports that at Naledi High the principal wished the pupils good luck, that the Action Committee's chairman, Tebello Motopanyane, stressed that the march must be disciplined and peaceful, and that Tsietsi Mashinini said the same at Morris Isaacson. The plan was for columns to gather pupils from other schools as they went. The Truth Commission was told the first groups set off at about 7 a.m.; it also heard that police opened fire at 8 a.m. on two schoolboys who were running to catch up with the marchers. By about 9 a.m., the Commission recorded, approximately 10,000 pupils had converged on the area of Orlando West High School.

Estimates of the crowd differ. South African History Online says 3,000 to 10,000; Newsweek and the Michigan exhibit say 10,000 to 20,000. South Africa Gateway counts 11 columns, up to 10,000 people by some estimates. Placards in English read "Down with Afrikaans" and "If we must do Afrikaans, Vorster must do Zulu".

Police barricaded the planned route, and the marchers took another. On the way, Mashinini climbed onto a tractor and told the crowd, in the words South Africa Gateway quotes, "We are not fighting." Police retreated to wait for reinforcements. At what is now Hector Pieterson Square, they stopped the column again.

The accounts of what happened next differ, and the sources say so. South Africa Gateway describes a white policeman throwing a tear gas canister into the front of the crowd and a policeman at the back setting a dog on the students, who threw stones at it. It says a single shot rang out and Hastings Ndlovu, 17 (other sources say 15), was hit; he died later in hospital. The Truth Commission's account is that after an appeal for calm by student leaders a contingent of police formed an arc in front of the marchers, a tear gas canister was thrown, the marchers threw stones, and the police opened fire. Two pupils were fatally wounded, and the first of them, the Commission wrote, was Hector Pieterson. Morobe told the Commission that the violence began only after the dog was set on the students and the shooting began; he said the later stone-throwing was an angry reaction and "never part of the plan".

Photographer Sam Nzima, quoted by South African History Online, said: "I saw a child fall down. Under a shower of bullets, I rushed forward and went for the picture. It had been a peaceful march, the children were told to disperse, they started singing Nkosi Sikelele. The police were ordered to shoot."

Sources differ on Pieterson's age. South African History Online and Newsweek say 12, the Truth Commission and the Michigan exhibit say 13. Pieterson was picked up and carried by Mbuyisa Makhubo, a fellow student, aged 18 according to Newsweek, with Pieterson's sister Antoinette Sithole running beside them. Sithole told the Commission that they reached a clinic where a doctor said nothing could be done, at about 10:30. South African History Online reports that a post-mortem found Pieterson was killed by a shot fired directly at him, not by a bullet "ricocheting off the ground" as the police claimed.

Nzima's photograph went round the world. Newsweek reports that Nzima was punished with 19 months of house arrest after it was published. Makhubo's mother told the Truth Commission that her family was severely harassed by police after the picture appeared, that Makhubo went into exile, and that nothing had been heard from him since he wrote to her from Nigeria in 1978.

With Pieterson's death, in the Commission's words, the protest changed "from a peaceful march into a violent confrontation". Pupils built barricades and attacked beer halls, bottle stores and administration buildings. Two officials of the West Rand Administration Board, Dr Melville Edelstein and a Mr Esterhuizen, were killed. The Michigan exhibit says a mob stoned Edelstein to death and hung a placard on him.

South Africa Gateway reports that more students were killed in clashes near Regina Mundi Church in Orlando and at a petrol station in Chiawelo, and that as police stopped them in one area the students carried the protest elsewhere. Many pupils who had not known about the march walked out of school at about noon into a township in flames. Dr Malcolm Klein, a trauma doctor at Baragwanath Hospital, later recalled the arrival of orderlies wheeling stretchers with the bodies of children, each with a red "Urgent Direct" sticker on the forehead. By the next day 1,500 heavily armed police were in Soweto, according to Michigan, and armoured police vehicles later known as "hippos" had begun moving in.

The Truth Commission's Volume 3 describes the Riot Unit, set up in early 1975, drawing on recruits with counter-insurgency training. One of them was Swanepoel, who gathered the first sixty men he could and led a fifty-eight-strong task force into Soweto in the first twenty-four hours. The Commission described him as having a long history of gross human rights violations as chief interrogator of the Security Branch. According to the Commission's regional profile, Swanepoel gave the crowd the order to disperse on 16 June and said later that he had taken up a policy of shooting to kill. In his own words, quoted by the Commission, he "used appropriate force" and that "broke the back of the organisers".

The Commission also found that many in the security establishment believed too little force had been used. Deputy Commissioner Wandrag held that officers who hesitated allowed "rioters gaining confidence and acting in an increasingly impudent and militant way". In its findings the Commission concluded that the police adopted a shoot-to-kill policy, and held Swanepoel and Deputy Commissioner Wandrag responsible for the excessive use of force that led to the deaths of more than 575 students, most of them under twenty-five. It also held the students responsible for the deaths of Edelstein and the other Administration Board official, while also blaming the police and the former state for the climate in which those killings happened. It also heard that in July the government closed schools in at least eighty townships, and that in August police raided schools looking for Student Representative Council leaders.

The day after the march, the government announced a one-person commission under Justice Cillié. Its first public hearing took evidence on damage and casualties. It counted 575 dead and 2,389 injured between 16 June 1976 and 28 February 1977, and attributed 451 deaths to police. South Africa Gateway, citing a different tally for the year, gives 3 907 injured, 2 389 of them by police, and about 5 980 arrests in the townships during 1976.

The Commission's conclusions, as quoted by the Truth Commission, were: "Bantu Education was not a cause of the riots. It was, to a certain degree, a cause of dissatisfaction; this dissatisfaction was to some extent stirred up and exploited by those bent on creating disturbances." It held the Soweto Students' Representative Council primarily responsible for the unrest not ending sooner. It said the police had acquitted themselves well and found no evidence of deliberate, impermissible assaults or indiscriminate use of firearms.

Morobe told the Truth Commission he believed the inquiry was set up to justify the shootings. He alleged collusion between police and the Commission in producing evidence against the student council, and said that after a December 1976 sweep he and others were interrogated and tortured at John Vorster Square and then made to read statements before the inquiry. He added that its conclusions underlay the 1978 sedition charges against leaders of the protest, himself included. These are his allegations, made to the Truth Commission.

The Truth Commission recorded that at least eleven people died in police custody in 1976 and fourteen in 1977. The Commission lists a ban in October 1977 on every Black Consciousness organisation and on two newspapers, The World and Weekend World, and adds that security personnel received legal indemnity backdated to 16 June 1976. Newsweek reports that the government withdrew the Afrikaans decree in July 1976. South African History Online says many students left South Africa to join the exiled liberation movements, and that pictures of police firing on the marchers caused international revulsion at the apartheid state. Newsweek says the United Nations Security Council was convened and denounced the "massive violence against and killings of the African people including schoolchildren".

The Truth Commission held a special hearing on the uprising in 1996, convened because it felt the number of statements it had received did not convey the event's significance. A Hector Pieterson memorial was put up in Orlando, two blocks from where he fell, and the Hector Pieterson Museum opened behind it in 2002. South Africa has observed 16 June as Youth Day since 1994.
